changes.question: My country should sell publicly owned commercial businesses to private owners.
changes.reason: Ho defended socialist reconstruction and the move toward socialism and communism; North Vietnamese ownership expanded through state enterprises and cooperatives. Cooperatives are not automatically government-owned. These actions make rejection of a general sale policy more likely than endorsement; they do not prove an answer to every modern ownership trade-off.

changes.question: Private ownership should be preferred when public and private providers could offer comparable cost, quality, and access.
changes.reason: Ho defended socialist reconstruction and the move toward socialism and communism; North Vietnamese ownership expanded through state enterprises and cooperatives. Cooperatives are not automatically government-owned. Comparable delivery does not establish a preference for private ownership over the public sector. A qualified rejection best fits selective public expansion, rather than claiming every business must be nationalised.

changes.question: Businesses important to national security should remain privately owned when government regulation can protect security interests.
changes.reason: Ho defended socialist reconstruction and the move toward socialism and communism; North Vietnamese ownership expanded through state enterprises and cooperatives. Cooperatives are not automatically government-owned. Strategic ownership was itself a policy instrument, so regulation alone is unlikely to have been regarded as sufficient grounds to retain private ownership in all security-sensitive businesses.

changes.question: A publicly owned business that repeatedly needs financial support should be sold to private owners rather than kept in public ownership.
changes.reason: Ho defended socialist reconstruction and the move toward socialism and communism; North Vietnamese ownership expanded through state enterprises and cooperatives. Cooperatives are not automatically government-owned. Financial support alone does not establish a presumption of sale; maintaining strategic capacity and social purposes makes a qualified rejection more likely. The record does not settle every loss-making firm.

similarity.reason: Ho Chi Minh (Leadership of the Democratic Republic of Vietnam, 1945–1969) and Indira Gandhi (Premierships, 1966–1977 and 1980–1984) are distinct individuals and periods. The largest difference is public-private: State and collective ownership expanded through land reform and socialist reconstruction. Counter-evidence: Early coalition and small producers were not immediately abolished; collective/cooperative ownership differs from national government ownership in precise questions. The peer's assessment instead records: Bank and industrial nationalisation, state-led strategic sectors and public broadcasting expanded ownership. Retain the independently recorded subjects and this evidence-based correction; do not alter responses to manufacture distance.

Ho Chi Minh (Leadership of the Democratic Republic of Vietnam, 1945–1969) and Indira Gandhi (Premierships, 1966–1977 and 1980–1984) are distinct individuals and periods. The largest difference is democracy-autocracy: Independence and popular sovereignty were declared, but opposition suppression and Communist Party predominance constrained competitive elections. Counter-evidence: Initial coalition institutions and the demand for reunification elections matter; revolutionary popular claims are not equivalent to equal opposition access. The peer's assessment instead records: Won elections and returned after defeat, but the Emergency curtailed opposition, delayed elections and sought to limit judicial constraints. Retain the independently recorded subjects and this evidence-based correction; do not alter responses to manufacture distance.
